name: Question 4
problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+x{y}^{′}-4y={x}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,x>0
$$

has the complimentary function ${y}_{c}(x)=\frac{A}{{x}^{2}}+B{x}^{2}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation. 

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the following result:* 

$$
\int {x}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=4x({x}^{2}-6)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+({x}^{4}-12{x}^{2}+24)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C
$$
worked_solution:
First, we reduce the differential equation to the form

$$
{y}^{″}+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=f(x).
$$

So, we divide both sides of the given equation by ${x}^{2}.$ We get

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{1}{x}{y}^{′}-\frac{4}{{x}^{2}}y=x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

We notice that the forcing term $f(x)=x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ Additionally, we're given the fundamental solutions:

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}},\,{y}_{2}(x)={x}^{2}
$$

First, let's compute the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{1}^{′}{y}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}({x}^{2})^{′}-{(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})}^{′}{x}^{2} \\  & =2x(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})-(-\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}){x}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{x}+\frac{2}{x} \\  & =\frac{4}{x}\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions  ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are independent. 

According to the method of variation of parameters, the particular solution of the differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={y}_{1}(x)u(x)+{y}_{2}(x)v(x),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}u(x) & =-\int \frac{f(x){y}_{2}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{4}\int {x}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{4}(4x({x}^{2}-6)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+({x}^{4}-12{x}^{2}+24)\operatorname{sin}⁡x), \\ v(x) & =\int \frac{f(x){y}_{1}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={y}_{1}(x)u(x)+{y}_{2}(x)v(x) \\  & =(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})(-\frac{1}{4}(4x({x}^{2}-6)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+({x}^{4}-12{x}^{2}+24)\operatorname{sin}⁡x))+({x}^{2})(\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =(-x+\frac{6}{x})\operatorname{cos}⁡x+(-\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+3-\frac{6}{{x}^{2}})\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & =(\frac{6}{x}-x)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+(3-\frac{6}{{x}^{2}})\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Given that the differential equation x2y″+xy′−4y=x3cos⁡x,x>0 has the complimentary function yc(x)=Ax2+Bx2, find the particular solution yp(x) to this equation.

Hint: You may wish to make use of the following result: ∫x4cos⁡xdx=4x(x2−6)cos⁡x+(x4−12x2+24)sin⁡x+C

a
yp(x)=(6−x2)cos⁡x+(x2−3)sin⁡x
b
yp(x)=(1x−x)cos⁡x+2xsin⁡x
c
yp(x)=(6x−x)cos⁡x+(3−6x2)sin⁡x
d
yp(x)=6xcos⁡x−xsin⁡x
e
yp(x)=2x2cos⁡x−(3−x)sin⁡x
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we reduce the differential equation to the form y″+P(x)y′+Q(x)y=f(x).

So, we divide both sides of the given equation by x2. We get y″+1xy′−4x2y=xcos⁡x.

We notice that the forcing term f(x)=xcos⁡x. Additionally, we're given the fundamental solutions: y1(x)=1x2,y2(x)=x2

First, let's compute the Wronskian: W(y1,y2)=|y1y2y1′y2′|=y1y2′−y1′y2=1x2(x2)′−(1x2)′x2=2x(1x2)−(−2x3)x2=2x+2x=4x≠0

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions y1(x) and y2(x) are independent.

According to the method of variation of parameters, the particular solution of the differential equation is

yp(x)=y1(x)u(x)+y2(x)v(x), where u(x)=−∫f(x)y2(x)W(y1,y2)dx=−14∫x4cos⁡xdx=−14(4x(x2−6)cos⁡x+(x4−12x2+24)sin⁡x),v(x)=∫f(x)y1(x)W(y1,y2)dx=14∫cos⁡xdx=14sin⁡x.

Thus, yp(x)=y1(x)u(x)+y2(x)v(x)=(1x2)(−14(4x(x2−6)cos⁡x+(x4−12x2+24)sin⁡x))+(x2)(14sin⁡x)=(−x+6x)cos⁡x+(−x24+3−6x2)sin⁡x+x24sin⁡x=(6x−x)cos⁡x+(3−6x2)sin⁡x.
